2d33992d-924e-4bf4-aa10-79171639ba7a,187351,why-love-can-be-so-unsexy,Why Love Can Be So… Unsexy,null,"The other day my friend Sam (not his real name, because Kenya is small and I enjoy being alive) said something that disturbed my inner Hollywood-trained relationship police.

He said, very casually, “I can’t wait to live in a bigger house. With more bedrooms. So that once in a while I can sleep in another room. Or my wife can. Just to get space.” I stared at him the way you stare at someone who has just announced they don’t believe in salt.
Another room?

My brain immediately opened the Netflix folder called Marriage Is Ending. In those movies, once you hear “guest room,” it’s over. Someone is cheating. Someone is drinking whiskey alone. Someone has already called their lawyer. Someone is about to say, “I just don’t feel seen.” So I did what modern romantics do: I panicked politely.

“Bro… what do you mean?” I asked. “Do you not love your wife? Isn’t sleeping together the whole point? Isn’t that what marriage is? Two bodies, one duvet, one destiny?” Sam looked at me the way your mother looks at you when you say you want to be a DJ.
He said, “I love her. And no, we're not fighting. I just want space sometimes. I want to miss her.”

I wasn't convinced that they were not fighting but later on, after going through a rabbit hole of romantic research and significant amounts of wine, I realized what my blindspot was; millennials are a generation taught by Hollywood to interpret everything in relationships as a sign.
Separate bedrooms? Sign.
Silence? Sign.
He didn’t post you? Sign.
She didn’t laugh at your joke? Sign.
He came home late? Sign, sign, sign.

Meanwhile, sometimes it’s not a sign. Sometimes it’s just… life. And bodies. And routine. And familiarity. And the fact that you can deeply love someone and still want to breathe without another warm human being exhaling on you.

But here’s the bigger point Sam accidentally stepped on: We are the first humans in history trying to keep desire alive for decades, for pleasure, with one person. Not because we need ten children. Not because sex is a woman’s marital duty. Or because the clan is watching. No. We want sex in the long term to be about pleasure, connection, and desire. And that’s a very modern ambition. Beautiful. Romantic. But also… extremely difficult.

Because modern love is basically telling one person, “Be my peace. Be my stability. Be my soft place to land. But also, keep me excited. Keep me curious. Surprise me. Do it for decades. And please don’t get tired. Thanksss.”

We have taken what an entire village used to provide, whether that's community, identity, support, laughter, status, or continuity, and dumped it onto one person’s shoulders like an overloaded mkokoteni. Then we look shocked when sex starts sounding like a work meeting.
Love wants closeness. Desire wants space.

Love reduces distance. Desire plays with it. Love wants certainty. Desire wants tension. Desire isn’t ownership, it’s the thrill of pursuit. It is movement. And like fire needs oxygen, desire needs air. It needs room to breathe. It needs distance, and here I'm not talking about divorce-level distance. Just enough distance for imagination to come back online.

In my romantic research I came upon a scintillating TED Talk in which the speaker mentioned that when you ask people, “When do you feel most drawn to your partner?” the answers are usually simple. Most follow this theme: When we’ve been apart, then we reunite. When I see them in their element. Confident. Focused. Doing their thing. When we’re surprised and we laugh together. When a different side of them shows up.

The pattern you'll notice in these responses is that even a small gap can bring back longing. It's not about new tricks. It’s about seeing the same person differently. We think novelty is technique. So we buy lingerie. But novelty isn’t about props. Novelty is about who you're allowed to be. What parts of you show up in those moments. It's about letting those parts of you that have been trapped under “responsible adult who pays bills” come out.
Neediness is not sexy

Let’s say this plainly, like adults, because we are adults. Neediness is not sexy. Wanting your partner is sexy. Needing your partner like oxygen is not sexy. Don't get me wrong, caretaking is beautiful. It brings out tenderness. It brings out devotion. But it is also, for many people, a powerful anti-aphrodisiac. Why? Because caretaking activates the parental brain. And the parental brain is not trying to breed. The parental brain is trying to keep everyone alive, hydrated, and vaccinated.

Turns out when couples say “We’re still best friends, we still love each other, but sex is dead,” you should not be shocked. Love can be strong while sex dies, and that doesn’t automatically mean the relationship is failing. Often it’s just that the couple has built a life that runs on responsibility. On home management, routines, and caretaking. Desire doesn’t thrive there. And kids make it worse: less sleep, less privacy, more interruptions, body changes, and a permanent sense of being on duty. Parenthood might be sacred, but it’s also where erotic life often gets shelved.
Sex is a place you go.

Animals have sex. Biology. Instinct. Humans have an erotic life. Which means sexuality transformed by imagination. We can have a whole night of pleasure and touch nobody. We can turn ourselves on with anticipation alone. We can experience desire while nothing is happening. Which is why sex isn’t just behavior. It’s a new language between you and your partner.

So the real question is not “how do we have more sex?” The real question is ""What do you seek in sex?"" Is it a place for you to feel adored? Maybe a place to be nasty? Or perhaps it's a place where you can be powerful. A place to surrender. A place to play with danger safely. Desire isn’t always sweet. It can come with jealousy, power, roughness, mischief, taboo, and sometimes a bit of selfishness too. Because the erotic mind is not politically correct nor does it care about good manners.
The most important question

People love asking: “What turns you on?” As if your partner is a remote control where you press a button and they receive an orgasm. It turns out the more adult question is “What turns me on?” Same question, just pointed at the right person. Because if you are dead inside, nobody can resurrect you with roses and a dinner reservation.

Do you turn yourself on when you feel alive? Or is it when you feel confident. Or when you’re in your element. Or when you’re not performing life for everyone else. Conversely, when do you turn yourself off? Is it when you feel unattractive? When you feel old? When you feel unseen? When your self-esteem is in the gutter? When you’re exhausted? When, exactly?

One thing I know about desire is that it is not only relational. It is also personal. If you're married or in a relationship already like my friend Sam, and you're wondering how to want what you already have, the good news is that it is possible, just not necessarily by spending more time together with your partner. If you want to rekindle the desire for what you already have, you first need to restore the conditions that nurture desire. That means space, mystery, play, sexual privacy, anticipation and yes, intention. The part about intention will annoy some people because it’s not romantic but here's the thing, committed sex is almost always premeditated. It's intentional and planned. Not because your love is fake but because your life is full. The myth of spontaneity is the biggest scam sold to our generation of Hollywood-inspired couples. That scene in the movie where desire falls from heaven while my person is folding laundry like God is my wingman sounds romantic. But long-term desire is something you cultivate and make room for.
Desire and Distance
Which brings me back to Sam and his extra bedroom dream.

Maybe the second bedroom isn’t a sign of a dying marriage. Maybe it’s a sign of a couple that understands something we’ve forgotten: You cannot desire what you never get to miss. Sometimes the sexiest thing you can do for your relationship is to create a little distance, not to punish, or to escape, or to threaten. But to breathe. To look at the same person with fresh eyes because maybe then, you will remember why you chose them first.

If you’re single, do not make your partner your whole universe. Keep your friendships. Keep your ambition. Keep your mystery. Keep your glow. Let them see you in your element. Let them miss you sometimes.

9ead4c51-153b-4e8e-9b7d-0ccd10e5c75e,187787,the-birth-of-the-visualizer,The Music Video Is Dead. Long Live the Visualizer.,null,"When Michael Jackson released the album Thriller in 1982, he completely changed what the industry at the time thought of music videos. From his song “Billie Jean” not being played on MTV due to racism to the song “Thriller” leading to the album being the best selling album of all time, Michael Jackson had transformed music videos from a relatively obscure function of music to a mainstream promotional and marketing tool. More than 40 years later, the world of music has changed completely. Streaming has taken over with physical sales diminishing, while music videos have been relegated to a mainstay for artists with large budgets. This shift in the visual aspect of music has left a gap that has quickly been filled by visualizers. Visualizers have quickly taken over the gap that was once filled by music videos. But what exactly is a visualizer and why did it suddenly come to take over the music industry?

To better understand visualizers, one has to understand the music consumption cycle. In the traditional music cycle, the album was king. An artist would release a single, push it to market and release an accompanying music video. This music video would work in tandem with the song to promote the upcoming album and many times would introduce fans to the visual concept of the album. Globally, artists like Kanye West, Beyonce and The Weeknd have had consistent visual themes across multiple videos for their albums. These visual themes create an avenue for the artist to better relay the overall concept of the album while being yet another creative tool for their expression. These music videos would often be played on music channels like MTV, Trace, Channel O and VH1. In the 2000s, The Beat on NTV was the premier destination for music videos in Kenya. Getting a placement on such channels and programs was almost a guarantee for your song to perform well commercially. After two or three singles, artists world release an album and due to the attention already generated by their singles and accompanying videos, the albums would perform well. Or so they hoped.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HUXWHkSJdFQ

Record companies understood the power of music videos to place artists before new audiences. They hoped that through music videos, audiences would want to be like the music star i.e. dress like them or talk like them. Most importantly, many audiences would want that t-shirt or jacket or shoes from their favourite artist’s music video thus increasing merchandise sales. At one point in the industry, music videos and the few avenues for them to be played were a guarantee for a hit song and a subsequent hit album. Just like many other things in entertainment, this all changed when the internet became a mainstream communication and entertainment tool.

When the internet went mainstream in the mid 2000s, the main concern was piracy. Services like Napster and Limewire caused shivers down the music industries’ spines. When YouTube was launched in 2005, it quickly became an independent way for artists to release and share their music. From then on, a new kind of star was born. The YouTube star. While still heavily relying on music videos, the music industry seemed to understand the power of the internet at this time. With the death of popular music programming like BET’s 106 & Park in the 2010s, YouTube provided a direct to consumer approach that had never been seen before. This disruption meant that consumers were not heavily reliant on program directors’ taste and label influence. Music was now a democratic endeavour. This surge in YouTube music videos made legitimate stars in the 2010s. Many artists got a spotlight when traditional labels and music programs did not believe in them. But like with all things, the more they change, the more they stay the same. With advertising being one of YouTube's main revenue models, the labels were able to buy back the access and control and by the late 2010s, the YouTube landscape looked like the TV scene in the 2000s. Audiences were fractured but were always susceptible to the influence of labels and their marketing budgets. This was once again about to change.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=djf-uvRiwa0

In this new age, albums weren't necessary. In fact, the whole consumption cycle especially for smaller artists was not reliant on albums. Singles ruled the era of YouTube and streaming. Even better, one could have a hit in the age of the internet without a music video. Many artists therefore put all their focus on making good songs that were not reliant on the traditional media machine. When 2020 came along, the world went into lockdown for the pandemic. This once again changed the music industry. TikTok was now the biggest social media platform. What made TikTok particularly subservient to the traditional media machine was its format. Videos were at first capped at 60 seconds. This short window gave creators an opportunity to find, utilise and maximise their creativity while keeping audiences glued to their screens. The relevance of music videos once again went down. What was left was user generated content that would push a song for an artist sometimes even without their knowledge. This left the music video to the big artists who had label access and budgets. For the smaller artists, you hoped your 10 second section would go viral before even releasing the full song. It is not uncommon to see parody videos and skits do better than the actual music video in this day and age.

And thus the visualizer was born. An invention of the mid 2010s especially in the electronic music scene, visualizers have always been part of the game. So when budgets don't align, it is easier to shoot a one minute low effort loop with your phone and pay an editor to put lyrics on the screen and have yourself a visualizer . Not a music video with complete sets and narratives but rather a cheap attention grabbing video to keep the listener engaged. Visualizers come in different tastes and flavours. From audio waveforms, to lyric videos, to short loops, to sometimes complete sets with artists miming, to b-roll footage of the artists performances and sometimes everyday life, there is no shortage of material for the artist to come up with a visualizer . With this, the music video is left for the ‘serious’ artists, those that are able to craft narrative and pay directors and actors on set.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=04GKMWEwe98

And even those serious artists have come to rely on visualizers. The only difference is you see the effort. For an artist to shoot a music video locally with an established director, one would need at least Kshs. 200,000. To have a lyric video made, one could get away with paying for a subscription to an AI model to do this for you while you slap a video shot on your phone at home as the background for a fraction of the cost. For independent and smaller artists, visualizers give them the freedom to express themselves on a budget while killing two birds with one stone. One, you give the audience a visual to keep them entertained. Two, you are able to give a lyric video with an added value while also banking on the song doing well to justify the 250k for a video. For big artists, they are able to test the waters of what works with the audience without the need for a big budget or pressure from labels to have a return on investment.

‘Nairobi’ by Marioo and Bien has no ‘official music video’. It however has an ‘official visualizer’ which currently sits at 49 million views on YouTube. The visualizer however is not a low budget endeavour by any means. It is low effort, but not low budget. With the props used in this video, it would qualify for a music video just a decade ago. But in 2026, it is a visualizer . Both artists appear on video with lyrics appearing on screen. For all intents and purposes, it is a music video with low effort. But at what point would Marioo and Bien have decided to shoot a music video? At one, two or three million views? They wouldn't need to because they put out a low effort visualizer to a hit and called it a day. Such big artists are afforded this luxury. Again where would this video be played? With YouTube being the biggest platform for music videos, programmes like The Beat have been forgotten. This gives artists the independence to put out visuals without the conditions and biases of gatekeepers. Essentially doing it on their own terms.

In Kenya, the gatekeepers have been the biggest benefactors of the industry. Stories exist of DJ Pinye denying opportunities to artists to have their songs on The Beat. For context, DJ Pinye was the producer and chief curator of The Beat on NTV. If your song made it to The Beat in 2006 up to the early 2010s, you could count yourself as having a hit. It would get picked up by radio and this would subsequently translate to shows which would bring in money. The threshold for quality was therefore very high. In DJ Pinye’s own words, he had to be harsh as he had limited airtime to play quality music and videos. This curation criterion then left such spaces at the mercy of either exceptional quality or financial muscle. If an artist was able to pay their way onto The Beat and other music programming, why wouldn't they? This gatekeeping was effectively neutralised by the internet and in effect by social media.
http://youtube.com/watch?v=Vy9lEJNQ3iE

While a new kind of gatekeeping with algorithms and playlists have come into effect, the assumed chance of getting a hit by sheer luck has brought in an influx of new music and musicians. Coupled with the low cost and high visibility of visualizers, artists seem to rely more and more on them. Without the threat of a high investment and no return, visualizers offer artists the ability to creatively express themselves with low effort and budget music videos doubling as lyric videos to satisfy the social media need for a quick shareable piece of media to act as a promotional tool. The music video is dead and the visualizer is alive and well. But for how long? With the global death of music programming on television, music videos are now more of an Avant Garde tool than a regular art form. Music videos now seem to be high budget endeavours that require an artist and label to fully buy into the idea. This leaves the low budget aspect of it to visualizers because audiences still need to see the artist.

The tide might turn again. Music programming on television may return but until then, it lives on the internet. The visual aspect of music is here to stay. But the terminology and expectation of both the audience and artists has shifted. Whether this is for the better is yet to be seen. What is undeniable however is the fact that we are living in the age of the music visualizer not the music video.",vicmuia,2026-02-23 18:24:03+00,null,"[{""name"":""Music"",""domain"":""category"",""nicename"":""music""}]","[{""name"":""Music Videos"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""music-videos""},{""name"":""Visualizer"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""visualizer""}]","{""description"":""To better understand visualizers, one has to understand the music consumption cycle. d68bc392-e173-46e8-8e67-b7dd7e75335d,187986,beef-the-rivalries-that-shaped-kenyan-music,Beef: The Rivalries That Shaped Kenyan Music,null,"Wherever people are competing for a crown, friction is bound to follow. After all, everyone wants to be the one wearing it. Few arenas illustrate this better than music, both internationally and locally. Over the years we have seen friends turn into foes, contemporaries into combatants and a wide array of artists take to the booth to trade insults for all manner of reasons. “Beef” as the streets call it, is as part of music culture as dancing and singing. From the very beginning, rivalry has run through the Kenyan music scene. As artists competed for audiences, influence and recognition, tensions were never far behind. Over time those tensions produced feuds, fallouts and public clashes that became part of the industry’s history. Some of those clashes have gone on to become part of the folklore of Kenyan music.
The Kapuka vs Genge Era

Kenyan pop music really began to take off in the early 2000s. While acts like Swahili Nation and Hardstone had earlier tried to carve out a distinctly Kenyan sound, it wasn’t until the turn of the millennium that something emerged which we could truly call our own. Studios and record labels popped up virtually overnight to create the music that would define a generation. By 2002, there were two record labels that would soon become giants of the game: Ogopa Deejays and Calif Records.

[caption id=""attachment_187987"" align=""alignnone"" width=""840""] While Ogopa Deejays perfected their pop ideologies, Calif Records were on the other end of the spectrum. Raw and raunchy, Calif appealed to the adults in the room. Nonini was their poster child at first, the king of innuendo and racy lyrics.[/caption]

Ogopa Deejays came first. Sleek, shiny and full of bubblegum pop aesthetics, they became the home of hitmakers like E-Sir, Nameless, Kleptomaniax, Longombas, Deux Vultures, and K-Rupt among many others. Ogopa was polished and radio friendly, the Midas touch that brothers Lucas and Francis Bikedo had was unprecedented. For a hot minute, they were Kenyan music. They dominated the charts like no one else. While Ogopa perfected their pop ideologies, Calif Records were on the other end of the spectrum. Raw and raunchy, Calif appealed to the adults in the room. Nonini was their poster child at first, the king of innuendo and racy lyrics. In time he became the first true star outside the Ogopa Deejays stable and with him began the healthy competition between the two record labels.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R7T5ZtiKMN4

From their base in the California neighbourhood of Eastleigh, Calif Records began shaping a sound that felt closer to the streets. Artists like Nonini, Mahatma, Lady S, Jimwat, Flexx and Jua Cali brought a swagger and irreverence that stood apart from the polished pop dominating the airwaves. Their songs leaned into cheeky innuendo and everyday Nairobi humour, giving the scene a new edge. Instead of love ballads they gave us steamy lyrics about bathroom romps. They eschewed the party anthems in favour of street stories and eventually grew just as big as Ogopa. Before long, the question became who really defined the Kenyan sound. Ogopa’s camp leaned into Kapuka, sometimes referred to as Boomba, while Calif planted its flag firmly in Genge. What followed was something of a Cold War between the two camps, each trying to outdo the other in the charts and on the airwaves. A Nameless release was quickly matched by a Nonini drop. Before umalize kusema ""Ati Kleptomaniax dropped a banger?"" Jua Cali would have already dropped one of his own. At one point, artists affiliated with Ogopa even attempted to introduce a blanket term for Kenyan music: “Kenyanese.” The idea never caught on and was eventually rejected by fans.
Cracks in the Concrete

For the most part, there was no real animosity in this rivalry, only a healthy sense of competition. Each camp pushed the other to do better, and in the process Kenyan music moved forward as both labels tried to outdo one another with every release. To the outside world everything seemed rosy. But beneath the surface, internal disagreements within the camps were beginning to simmer, threatening to undo what had taken years of work to build.

The first major cracks began to show when disagreements between Ogopa Deejays and several of its top artists reached a boiling point. Deux Vultures, Longombas, Mr. Googz and Vinnie Banton publicly announced that they were leaving the label to form the short-lived outfit Bad Man Camp alongside a number of other artists. Widely regarded as Kenya’s first pop supergroup, Bad Man Camp would release only one song before the core members eventually reconciled with Ogopa Deejays and returned to the label.

Calif Records, however, were not as fortunate. The label lost its leading star, Nonini, after disagreements with management over a range of issues. The fallout appears to have had a longer tail; years later Nonini has continued to reference the dispute, including recent public comments about former Calif Records head Clemmo on social media. Unfortunately, by 2012, barely a decade into their reign, both labels had become shadows of their former selves, slowly fading into obscurity.
Keeping It All on Wax

While Ogopa and Calif dominated the charts, other artists were beginning to carve out their own space in the industry, and not all of them appreciated the polished pop sensibilities of Kapuka. Among the most vocal critics were K-South, the hard-hitting rap duo made up of Bamboo and Abbas Doobeez, the latter so fond of beef you would think he lived in a slaughterhouse. Real and raw, the pair told street stories drawn from life in Kariobangi South.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rCHpKMw4yoI

Bamboo went on record criticizing what he saw as the growing commercial focus of Kapuka, taking aim at artists associated with Ogopa Deejays. The criticism eventually found its way into the studio with the release of the now-seminal diss track “Kapuka This, Kapuka That,” in 2004; a record that sent ripples across the entire industry. The Bhangra-infused track landed like a grenade on the streets, pulling no punches as K-South aired their grievances about the direction Kenyan music was taking. Up until that point the rivalry in the industry had largely been playful, a contest fought through chart positions and radio spins. But with “Kapuka This, Kapuka That,” the tone shifted. There would be no more friendly competition. Everything was on wax now.

As much as “Kapuka This, Kapuka That” is remembered as a generational track, the Kapuka camp would respond with what many consider one of the greatest songs in Kenyan music history. The response came, still in 2004, in the form of “Tuendelee” by Kleptomaniax, and the record took the entire country by storm. A pop masterpiece that still commands attention years later, the Kleptomaniax trio used the track to fire back at K-South, dressing down their rivals and even airing some of their alleged exploits in public, including the now infamous line about nightclub bathroom escapades (“…kumangana kila mahali kama mambuzi…”). Tuendelee did something that very few diss tracks can do, it achieved crossover success. The song became such a massive radio hit that many listeners eventually forgot it was even a diss track. Tuendelee proved that Kapuka wasn’t just radio friendly singles, it could also be as sharp and cutting as hip-hop when it needed to be. There is a certain irony in the fact that one of the biggest radio records in Kenyan music history was, at its core, a diss track.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eqfm3rj7lE8
Abbas K뫿

In the aftermath of Tuendelee, beef wasn’t on the menu as much as one might have expected. But one man kept the spirit of confrontation alive in the industry. Abbas K뫿, formerly of K-South and also known as Doobiez, seemed to find himself in one feud or another throughout his career. From artists, promoters and radio presenters, no one was spared from his ire. He famously had beef with Jua Cali, at one point referring to him dismissively as “Solar Boy”. Between the late 2000s and early 2010s, he was involved in a highly publicized back and forth with Octopizzo. But Abbas’s most significant feud would come much closer to home, with his one-time friend and collaborator, Chiwawa.

Chiwawa and Abbas had collaborated on a number of tracks over the years until their relationship took a dramatic turn. Abbas alleged that Chiwawa was responsible for his separation from his wife. Chiwawa denied the accusation but this did little to calm the situation. Tensions started to escalate in 2009 and soon it was full blown war between the two artists for months. Diss tracks began to surface, interviews grew increasingly inflammatory, and public opinion became divided on whether this was real or staged beef meant to revive both artists' careers. Eventually the back-and-forth culminated in a live show in July of 2010, where the two faced off on stage in a rap battle to settle the matter once and for all. By the end of the night, Abbas had been declared the winner but surprisingly the organizers didn’t award him his prize money after Chiwawa complained about the outcome. Abbas was always seemingly involved in a feud or falling out. Where some saw recklessness, others saw courage. One thing was undeniable: Abbas was always with the smoke.
Everyone Wants to Be The King

Sometimes beef begins with the smallest of provocations, as was the case with Prezzo and Jaguar. Prezzo had long styled himself as the king of luxury, projecting an image of excess and opulence and even naming his crew Cash Money Brothers (CMB). For years he wore the crown as Kenya’s undisputed king of bling. In 2010, Jaguar, the Kenyan music artist, now turned politician, saw things differently. He told everyone who would listen that he was the new king of bling. Prezzo, never one to shy away from confrontation, took the challenge personally. Calling into the legendary Hits Not Homework radio show, he publicly belittled Jaguar, dismissing him as a nobody trying to gain attention by invoking his name. Just like that, another chapter of beef in the Kenyan music industry had begun. On top of diss tracks, public insults were exchanged, and accusations, including allegations of drug addiction, were thrown back and forth as the feud intensified threatening to spill beyond music. Eventually, Tanzanian artist A.Y. stepped in to mediate a truce between the two camps. The intervention worked. The artists reconciled 8 years later in 2018 and would go on to record a song together, finally burying the hatchet.
[caption id=""attachment_187990"" align=""alignnone"" width=""1334""] Kenyan artist Octopizzo performing in front of a crowd in Nairobi. | Image: Octopizzo[/caption]
Octopizzo vs Khaligraph Jones

While others bury the hatchet, others insist that the beef must always remain fresh. Such is the case between Octopizzo and Khaligraph Jones since around 2013-2014 when tensions were brewing between the two artists. Two of the most iconic rap artists in Kenya’s history are also two who, it seems, may never see eye to eye.

The origins of the beef are allegedly traced back to a famous Words And Pictures (WAPI) event, where Khaligraph defeated Octopizzo in a rap battle. According to many accounts, Octopizzo did not take kindly to the loss. This led to Khaligraph dropping ""I Run 254"" in 2014, a track that painted Octopizzo as a jealous loser who relied on his girlfriend for financial support to grow his career. This was the first salvo in what would become one of the most persistent rivalries in Kenyan hip-hop.
Over the years Khaligraph has occasionally hinted at a desire to move past the feud. On the track “Yes Bana,” he even rapped:
“Na mi sina beef na Ohanga (Sipendi)
Ohanga hunitaki kwa nini? (Yes bana)
Mbona usifanye traki na mimi? (Yes bana)
Tutop hizi chart za mjini (Yes bana).”

Octopizzo, however, has repeatedly made it clear that reconciliation is not on his agenda, publicly stating that he neither likes nor respects Khaligraph as a person. For now, it appears that the dream collaboration between the two may never come to pass.
Femi One vs Njeri

Beef isn’t just reserved only for the men in the arena. It easily crosses gender and genre lines to prove that animosity is a universal language. In 2016 rapper Femi One dropped Pilau Njeri, a track aimed at fellow rapper Njeri. The video opens with a clip of Njeri speaking about how Femi One inspires her. Njeri had previously spoken about how much Femi One inspired her, only to later turn around and start talking smack. Femi flipped those very words against her, using her rival’s own praise as the opening before dismantling her on the track.
[caption id=""attachment_24578"" align=""alignnone"" width=""1920""] Kenyan artist Femi One. | Image: Femi One[/caption]

While Femi One took shots at other rappers such as Noti Flow, Njeri bore the brunt of her fury and she later responded in kind. Tensions between the two would later ease, but the moment had already made its mark. It was the first time two female artists had openly gone at each other on record and that set the entire industry buzzing. These days Njeri’s response track is almost impossible to find, despite being a particularly hilarious rebuttal at the time. Femi One, for her part, has occasionally spoken about the fallout from the beef in interviews nearly a decade later.
Bahati vs Willy Paul

Around the same time, the gospel world was rocked by a falling out between two of the biggest artists in the Gospel genre. Bahati and Willy Paul, once friends, publicly fell out in 2015 after Bahati alleged that Willy Paul, together with producer Teddy B, had been stealing his songs. While the two eventually buried the hatchet over that dispute, tensions flared again in 2021 when Willy Paul took to social media to disparage Diana, Bahati’s spouse, and even claimed that he had been in a relationship with her before she met Bahati. The accusations reignited the feud, with both camps trading jabs online and tensions spilling across social media. Eventually the two artists mended relations and even released two tracks together in 2024. Whether the peace will hold, however, remains to be seen.
Toxic Lyrikali vs Buruklyn Boyz
Time flies, days turn to decades but the beef remains eternal, it never really dies; it simply moves from one artist to the next.
For a while, the Kenyan music scene had gone without a truly explosive rivalry. Until very recently.
[caption id=""attachment_145133"" align=""alignnone"" width=""2560""] Kenyan artist Toxic Lyrikali. | Image: Toxic Lyrikali[/caption]

Ever since getting his big break in 2025, rapper Toxic Lyrikali has been on a mission to feud with as many people as possible. From Kasa Boss to Parroty to Tipsy Gee, Toxic has had no shortage of rivals. He has even shown that he is willing to confront people in public, at one point running up on Tipsy Gee with a whole squad of associates and forcing Tipsy Gee to apologize on camera. His current feud with Buruklyn Boyz, however, has taken things to another level and has the whole country talking. The dispute reportedly began after Toxic accused Mr. Right of the Buru Buru duo of borrowing his dancehall style on the track “Shillings.” Toxic took to the internet to throw shade but the Buruklyn Boyz were not about to let the accusation slide. Response videos, social media posts and diss tracks have been traded back and forth as fans choose sides between the two camps. Even with the beef still ongoing, there is no mistake that this is the most relevant the two acts have been in recent memory.

The Anatomy of Beef

Whether driven by intense professional competition, genuine personal conflict or even as a clever marketing strategy, feuds between artists have long been a hallmark of the music industry and Kenya is no exception. Beef keeps artists relevant and quite often, keeps them rich. As long as people are talking about you, you are winning. Attention is the most important currency in the music game and the more of it you command, the better positioned you are. Some of the biggest songs and defining moments in Kenyan music have emerged from competition between artists and record labels, each trying to assert dominance within the industry. Start a Book Club,null,"I am a lifelong collector of written materials and similar paraphernalia so I have been junk journaling. Healthy U would be horrified to learn what I’ve done to the little free magazines that I so excitedly take every time I buy incense sticks. I’m using my old diaries. I’m too attached to toss them as they are so I’m turning them into something else while making it ok for me to throw out what remains after each ‘journaling’ session. This is knitting for me. It is not journaling or reading, the other two things I do. It’s not social either and while I’ve had fun doing blackout poems and destroying old papers, I fear I need something more.
So let’s you and I talk ourselves into starting or joining a book club. There are four things to consider.
The Books

One of the best parts of hanging out with bookish people is that they always have recommendations. And in a book club (yours maybe) each member could take a turn choosing what book to read next. When you get this book and start reading it, you will not be hounded by the urge to give it up and clickbait because you have a job beyond just reading it. You have to decide what it says about the person who chose it. Cold and remote judgement in a scholarly but casual setting. Doesn’t that just send a tingle down your spine?

If you want to learn more about a certain topic, a book club that picks books according to set categories or topics can force you to do it. Again, the subtle social pressure will work wonders. For example, if you would like to understand why history repeats itself like a turning wheel, crushing Africans under it, you might consider the Noname Book Club (NBC, so I don't have to type out the whole name again). The club meets at Cheche Book Store in Nairobi once a month on Sundays.
The Community

If you are anything like me, you do not belong to a chama or a praise & worship group or the core group of friends at your job. You just read and keep to yourself. People ask you stuff when they cannot be bothered with their little AI boyfriend. After you answer and lose the battle against over-explaining, they leave you to your book. I’m saying you need to find your people.

Book club meetings have a set agenda, so you can prepare in advance. No one is going to bring a random person or bottle into it. There could be wine but only if everyone has a set of those fancy pots that you get from Kamukunji. Purchased with own (or life partner’s money) on site. Anyone else making wine a part of book clubs cannot be trusted to do so responsibly. With each meeting you will be making connections and building history with people who love the thing you love but in different ways, so it is always interesting.
The Reading

There are different kinds of reading. The kind of reading where you have to form an opinion about the book and articulate it to others is the best. Even a bodice ripper takes on new colours and dimensions when you have considered what it is to you and what you might have to say about it, if anything. Critical or analytical reading will probably lead to uncovering surprising insights about yourself. You can interrogate how you think by connecting thoughts and feelings to what is on the page. Then, when others give their take on it, you’ll have an even richer understanding of how similar or different your thinking is.
This might lead to a more reasonable consideration of the opinions of others and having more nuanced takes. If this is a concern, just up your TikTok screen time and they will cancel each other out.
The Events
I already mentioned the NBC Sunday meeting at Cheche and unless you're new to this, you will also have your other regular book club meeting. There’s also;
<ul>

column2: • Nairobi Litfest which is in its fifth year. That’s in June, so write that down.
• The African Book Fair by Soma Nami. You missed it last year, promise yourself never again.
• Kenya Museum Society pop-up market and book sale in March.

column1: There are also trips to bookshops, thrifting, and browsing other people’s bookshelves looking for titles. All of which might be better to attend as a group. At least it seems that way from the dark corner I usually lurk in. You would not believe the treasures hiding in the nooks and crannies of our once proudly learned nation. There might even be non-book club related fun to be had. Friendships and rivalries, crushes and embarrassments, and all the stuff of life.

91bdd766-21fd-4aa1-9d95-bf67ad8dd2ad,188042,what-to-know-about-the-proposed-copyright-bill,What to Know About the Proposed Copyright Bill,null,"For over two decades, Kenya’s creative heartbeat has been governed by a 2001 legal framework designed for an era of cassette tapes and physical books. Now, a sweeping new legislative proposal, the Copyright and Related Rights Bill, 2026, seeks to drag these laws into the 2020s. If passed, this bill will not just be a minor update; it represents a total overhaul of how artists are paid, how piracy is fought, and how disputes are settled in the digital age. Here is a breakdown of what is changing and what it means for creators and the public.
A More Powerful ""Authority"" and a New Court

The most visible change is the transformation of the regulator. The familiar Kenya Copyright Board (KECOBO) would be replaced by the Kenya Copyright Authority (KCA). While the name change seems cosmetic, the KCA is granted expanded supervisory powers, particularly over the often-criticized Collective Management Organizations (CMOs).

Beyond supervising CMOs, the Kenya Copyright Authority would have a wider day-to-day toolkit: it is tasked with voluntary registration, establishing a National Rights Registry, overseeing frameworks for royalties and private copying remuneration, and even issuing copyright compliance certificates to users of copyright works (in consultation with licensed CMOs). It is also explicitly empowered to impose administrative fines and charge fees and levies for services under the Act.

Even more significant is the creation of the Copyright Disputes Tribunal. Currently, disputes are handled by a ""Competent Authority"" appointed by a Minister. The new Tribunal would be a more formal body appointed by the Judicial Service Commission and chaired by a person qualified to be a High Court judge. This is a massive win for transparency and legal rigor in settling fights over ownership and royalties.
A National Rights Registry

One of the Bill’s most practical changes is a proposed Voluntary National Rights Registry. It would record rights holders and their works, make registry data publicly accessible, and crucially, treat registration as prima facie evidence of ownership or licensing. The Bill also links the registry to litigation by saying it can facilitate claims for statutory damages, and even record security interests in copyright works, basically treating copyright like an asset that can be pledged. Registration stays optional, and not a condition for protection, but it could become the fastest way to prove your claim when disputes arise.
Extended Protection: The 70-Year Shift

Under current law, photographers and filmmakers see their copyright expire 50 years after their work is made or published. The new bill proposes to extend this protection to 70 years for photographs, audio-visual works, and sound recordings.
<ul>

column2: • The Good: Creators and their heirs can benefit from their works for an extra two decades.
• The Bad: It keeps culture out of the ""public domain"" (where anyone can use it for free) for much longer.

column1: Quiet Change: The Public Domain May Finally Be “Free”

The current Copyright Act contains a rarely discussed clause: even when a work falls into the public domain, its use is still “subject to the payment of such fees as may be determined by the Minister.” The proposed Bill takes a cleaner position. It states that public-domain works “may be used without restriction,” and then defines what qualifies (expired term, rights renounced in writing, or foreign works not protected in Kenya).
A Quiet Ownership Shift: Commissioned Work Defaults Could Flip
Under the current Act, commissioned works are often treated as automatically transferred to the commissioner (subject to agreement), which has long shaped how creatives negotiate contracts.

The Bill proposes a different default: for commissioned work, the author retains ownership unless the commissioning contract expressly transfers copyright to the commissioner. That one change could strengthen creators at the contract stage, especially in advertising, photography, design, and film.
Digital Justice: Takedowns and Site-Blocking
In the current law, there are no specific ""safe harbor"" rules for the internet. The new bill finally addresses the ""Wild West"" of the web by introducing Safe Harbors for Online Intermediaries.

But safe harbor comes with conditions. The Bill requires online intermediaries to implement a repeat infringer policy with user notification, violation tracking, and account termination after multiple verified infringements. In other words, platforms get liability protection, but only if they actively police repeat offenders.
What A Valid Takedown Notice Looks Like

Also, the takedown system is more structured than a simple “remove in 48 hours.” A valid takedown notice must include specific details and must be copied to the Authority and the Communications Authority of Kenya. Once a valid notice is received, the intermediary must notify the person responsible for the content within 24 hours, and the default expectation is that the content is disabled within 48 hours, unless a counter-notice is filed.

Finally, the Bill introduces a formal counter-notice process: if the uploader disputes the takedown, they can file a counter-notice (with a sworn declaration) and copy it to the Authority. This is meant to reduce abuse, but it also means takedown disputes become a regulated workflow, not just a platform customer-care issue.
New Ways for Artists to Get Paid
The bill introduces several modern economic mechanisms that simply didn't exist in the 2001 Act:
<ul>

column2: • Artist’s Resale Right: For the first time, visual artists (painters, sculptors) would retain an inalienable right to a 5% share of the proceeds every time their original work is sold commercially through an auction or gallery.

• Ring-back Tune Fairer Split: The bill explicitly mandates that 52% of revenue from ring-back tunes must go directly to the copyright owner, limiting the share taken by telecommunication operators and content providers.
• Private Copying Levy: The existing levy on blank CDs and tapes is expanded to include modern devices and even online platforms that enable users to store or download copies for private use.

column1: Orphan works: a legal path for cultural materials that have “missing owners”

The Bill proposes a framework for “orphaned works,” where copyright still exists but the author is unknown or the rights holder cannot be traced. After a diligent search, a user can apply to the Authority for a non-exclusive licence to use the work, subject to terms. If the rights holder later emerges, they may be entitled to benefits from the use. For archivists, publishers, and documentary makers, this could unblock a lot of Kenya’s cultural material that currently sits in legal limbo.
Reversion rights: “Use it or lose it” for exclusive licenses

The Bill gives creators a stronger hand against exclusive licensees who sit on rights: if the exclusive licensee fails to exercise a granted right and that failure harms the copyright owner’s legitimate interests, the owner can revoke the right, and that right of revocation “shall not be waived in advance.” The Bill also states that if a licensee becomes insolvent, the licence terminates by operation of law, and the copyright owner can retrieve control of further distribution.
Copyright as collateral

In a more business-minded move, the Bill explicitly allows copyright to be used as security for a loan or obligation, by written agreement, enforceable under laws governing movable property. This is the kind of clause that can quietly change how creators, labels, publishers, and investors think about IP value.
Balance: Fair Use and Accessibility
It’s not all about enforcement. The bill modernizes ""exceptions,"" making it easier for certain groups to use content without permission:
<ul>

column2: • Persons with Disabilities: Following the international Marrakesh Treaty, the bill allows for the creation of accessible format copies (like Braille or audiobooks) for those with print disabilities without infringing copyright.

• Learning and Public Access Institutions: The Bill also expands exceptions for learning and public access institutions. Non-commercial educational establishments can copy limited extracts and share works with defined communities of learners via secure networks, while libraries, archives, and museums are allowed preservation copies, replacements, and even limited e-book lending mechanics. But there is a clear caveat: some educational uses are not permitted if a relevant licensing scheme exists and the institution “knew or ought to have known” about it.

• Data Mining: New provisions allow for Text and Data Analysis for non-commercial research, a crucial update for the age of AI and big data. To avoid confusion, the Bill frames text and data analysis as a limited permission: it allows copying for computational analysis for research only where the person has lawful access to the work, and it treats those copies as infringing if used for other purposes or dealt with beyond the permitted research. That wording is likely to matter as Kenya’s AI and research ecosystem grows, because it draws a line around what counts as legitimate non-commercial analysis.

column1: Fair use, but in Kenyan legal language: Fair dealing gets clearer

The Bill keeps Kenya’s fair dealing tradition but modernizes it by explicitly recognizing purposes like parody, caricature, pastiche, and satire, and by spelling out the factors a court must weigh, including the purpose of use, amount used, and market impact. It’s a small drafting move that could matter a lot for commentary culture, criticism, and remix-adjacent creativity.
Private copying becomes a consumer right, not just a levy

The Bill explicitly protects private, non-commercial copying for things like backup, format-shifting, and secure storage, and it states that any contractual term restricting these copies is unenforceable. This is a direct hit on “you may not copy” boilerplate terms that try to override the law.
Stronger Punishments for Pirates

For those caught infringing, the stakes are getting much higher. The bill introduces Statutory Damages, allowing courts to award between KES 200,000 and KES 1.5 million per work, even if the actual financial loss is hard to prove. The Bill’s statutory damages structure is also flexible in how courts can award them: a court may award a figure per work/performance, or a single figure for all works in the action, depending on how the case is framed and proven. It also states that where infringement is unknowing, the plaintiff is entitled only to statutory damages, and it explicitly allows punitive damages for “flagrant” infringement, defined as willful or large-scale infringement causing significant harm. It also grants the Authority the power to impose administrative fines for minor breaches without going through a full criminal trial.
The Verdict

The Bill is, at its core, an attempt to drag Kenya’s copyright system into the digital present. It promises creators sharper tools: clearer fair dealing rules, tougher online enforcement, a resale right for visual artists, and new mechanisms that make royalties and ownership easier to track, prove, and collect. But it also widens the state’s reach into the internet layer and introduces new levies and compliance obligations that could raise costs, encourage platforms to take down content too quickly, and concentrate significant power in a single regulator.

If Parliament passes it in its current form, Kenya will be opting for a more forceful copyright future. That future could meaningfully increase earning power across the creative economy, but only if the new Authority operates transparently, tariffs and levies are disciplined and evidence-based, and takedown and blocking powers are applied carefully rather than aggressively.

d8174ecd-064f-435d-8210-0aff2571f55c,204392,album-review-mtoto-wa-khadija-by-mejja,Album Review: Mtoto wa Khadija by Mejja,null,"On Thursday 5th March, Kenyan artist Mejja, born Major Nameye Khadija, held a listening party at the EABL Microbrewery in Ruaraka. Industry insiders and loyal fans were treated to new music from the veteran rapper. Coming into the event, one could feel the anticipation. What would an industry veteran 20 years into his career have to say in an album? For an artist well known for singles, what would an album sound like? The crowd was eager even before Mejja stepped onto the stage to give an exclusive listen of ‘Mtoto wa Khadija’. On that rainy Thursday evening, the expectations for what a debut album is or could be, subtly shifted. After almost 20 years in music, Mejja did it his way, he understood his audience, he understood his sound and most importantly, he understood his own limitations as an artist and as a rapper.
[caption id=""attachment_186472"" align=""alignnone"" width=""640""] Mejja’s solo hooks across the album are notably laid-back.[/caption]

During his Calif Records days, Mejja was renown as an vivid storyteller. His songs revolved around everyday life in a hilarious and relatable way. Since his debut single ‘Jana Kuliendaje’, Mejja has been the go-to storyteller of the Kenyan music industry, rhyming relatable bars that were almost always assured to connect with his fans. The next phase of his career would be the most defining as he moved to form a trio with Madtraxx and Kid Kora. This union d믭 ""The Kansoul"" paved the way for Mejja to continue churning out hits alongside his companions. It was at this time that Mejja shifted tact to predominantly becoming a featured artist. He became an artist whose most outstanding moments required him to be standing next to someone.
[wk_release id=""669""]

Although he experienced a renaissance in the 2020s, his place as a singles-releasing, featured artist was cemented. This positive feedback loop of never having to stand alone and be judged for his work was evident in this debut album. Out of 13 tracks, only 3 have Mejja by himself.  ‘Motion’ which comes in as the fifth track on the album sees the Nyeri-born rapper reminisce on his former days in the ghetto while contrasting to his current life circumstances. In what's a common thread within the album, the theme of Mejja losing it all and going back to poverty sees Mejja comment on his hustle in ‘Mboka’, another of his solo tracks. This song is particularly reminiscent of his days with The Kansoul with a dancehall-inspired beat and flow. Mejja’s 3rd and final solo song ‘Mmea’ is an ode to marijuana. The reggae beat on this track offers inspiration into what an exploration of other genres would mean for the veteran rapper. His very laid back delivery is an almost deliberate attempt at showcasing the effects of this (un)holy herb.
Featured

Mejja has become a master of his craft and an avid rapper whose simple metaphors reflect a very Kenyan way of life. However, while his features may be one of the standout aspects of his career, to see him come into his long-awaited debut album and be carried mostly by features is a little underwhelming as one would expect the Calif alumnus to rely on his experience and wisdom as a Kenyan music legend, to craft an apt album surrounding his circumstances. There are flashes of this in songs such as ‘Kauoga Flani’ featuring Scar Mkadinali, who despite being a phenomenal rapper, has increasingly leaned into shapeshifting through borrowed styles from other artists. Here, he delivers one of the album’s standout verses while channeling the cadence and energy of Jamaican artist Tommy Lee. Manifest, featuring Toxic Lyrikali, captures a younger, fresher-faced Toxic taking on the kind of beat he now sounds far more at home on, though here his voice still lacks the weight, experience, and maturity it would later gain. Mejja has said the track was recorded nearly two years ago, back when Toxic was still new on the scene. As the album’s lead single, Manifest once again finds Mejja wrestling with the irony of feeling like he still hasn’t fully made it, despite already being one of Kenya’s most recognizable rappers.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AQJyESOWMB8

Mental, featuring Khaligraph Jones, finds Mejja and the OG wrestling with the treachery of Nairobi’s streets. Khaligraph sounds just as comfortable rapping in Swahili here as he does in English or Dholuo, a reminder of the ease and command with which he moves across languages.

Mejja’s solo hooks across the album are notably laid-back. In an almost meditative mode, he leans on sparse one-liners that drift in to fill the hook space rather than dominate it. Siaka, one of the album’s standout tracks, finds Mejja and Uganda’s Fik Fameica trading verses over a dancehall beat, with Mejja anchoring the song through one of his characteristically simple hooks. Since its release, the track has emerged as the album’s clear breakout on TikTok, buoyed by the kind of dance challenges that often gather around a genuine hype record.

The opening track ‘Toxic’ with Shee and the 10th track ‘Naskia (ooh)' with Dyana Cods sees Mejja play into his lover boy aesthetic. ‘Toxic’ deals with heartbreak while ‘Naskia’ deals with sex, a particularly enjoyable subject for Mejja.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xSWwTo-8wHA

By the time ‘Vulai’ the last track on the album featuring Ndovu Kuu and Zzero Sufuri comes around, the album feels more like a playlist compilation assembled from different moods, moments, and impulses, than one cohesive project with a definite direction in mind. At the listening party, Mejja said the album was three years in the making, which only makes its lack of a clear, cohesive direction feel even more glaring. In later interviews, Mejja spoke about how nervous he was to finally present the album to fans at the listening party, and the drawn-out process behind it perhaps hints at some of that hesitation. Taken individually, many of the songs deliver the familiar pleasures of a Mejja track, but the long gaps between their making and eventual assembly into one project raise harder questions about cohesion and intent. For an artist of Mejja’s stature to pull together 13 songs recorded across three years and frame them as an album, the result leaves you searching for a stronger sense of who Mejja is at this moment, or even who this project wants him to be.

Ultimately, ‘Mtoto Wa Khadija’ feels less like a carefully crafted debut album and more like an effort to keep up with the times and maintain relevance. It does not quite come together as a sonically unified body of work. Still, for all its shortcomings, Mejja remains one of the enduring standard-bearers of Genge, still carrying that legacy forward, still unmistakably Mtoto wa Khadija.",vicmuia,2026-04-07 15:55:40+00,null,"[{""name"":""Album Reviews"",""domain"":""category"",""nicename"":""album-reviews""}]","[{""name"":""Calif Records"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""calif-records""},{""name"":""Dyana Cods"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""dyana-cods""},{""name"":""Khaligraph Jones"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""khaligraph-jones""},{""name"":""Mejja"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""mejja""},{""name"":""Scar Mkadinali"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""scar-mkadinali""},{""name"":""The Kansoul"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""the-kansoul""},{""name"":""Toxic Lyrikali"",""domain"":""post_tag"",""nicename"":""toxic-lyrikali""}]","{""title"":""Album Review: Mtoto wa Khadija by Mejja | WAKILISHA"",""ogTitle"":""Album Review: Mtoto wa Khadija by Mejja | WAKILISHA"",""canonical"":""https://wakilisha.africa/album-review-mtoto-wa-khadija-by-mejja/"",""description"":""At the listening party, Mejja said the album was three years in the making, which only makes its lack of a clear, cohesive direction feel even more glaring. 769cfe2d-3000-4b32-bfc6-d1002ce9bf95,205621,album-review-now-its-experience-talking-blinky-bill-muthoni-drummer-queen,Album Review: Now It's Experience Talking by Blinky Bill and Muthoni Drummer Queen,null,"As solo artists, Blinky Bill and Muthoni Drummer Queen have been pushing steadily against the old preconception that Kenyan music exists on the less daring region of the spectrum.

On all their solo projects, they happily explore the quirks of sonic exploration, establishing themselves as some of the most forward thinking and experimental artists in the Kenyan scene. Blinky Bill and MDQ have been frequent collaborators over the years, appearing on so many tracks together in recent memory, whether on posse cuts such as Party Nation or on underrated album gems such as Gong Gong. Eventually, after years of collaboration, it was only a matter of time until we got the joint album.
[caption id=""attachment_205632"" align=""alignnone"" width=""1400""] Album artwork for 'Now It's Experience Talking' by Blinky Bill and Muthoni Drummer Queen[/caption]

These features and collabs are the foundation that holds up Now It's Experience Talking and allows each artist to shine. The duo's long history together has helped them sharpen each other’s skills and know each other’s strengths which empowers them to hit a bit more of a stride on Now It’s Experience Talking. This isn't a MDQ-on-Blinky Bill beats project. In this album, both artists playfully trade the lead vocalist role on the project while the production, helmed by Blinky is aided by Dillie and Manchild, who add an extra layer of bounce and experimentation to the overall feel of the sound.
[wk_release id=""1095""]

Throughout the project, everyone involved in the production shows a clear willingness to take creative risks, even if a few moments do not quite land. But the LP’s shortcomings are largely outweighed by the risks that do pay off. And the biggest risk of all is its refusal to be bound by expectation. The duo shows little interest in sounding trendy, or in recreating the familiar chemistry of their previous collaborations. Instead, Now It’s Experience Talking becomes something else entirely, as any successful collaboration should. This can be traced both to the artists’ willingness to push the sonic envelope and to the length of the record’s gestation. More than five years passed between conception and release, giving the project time to arrive with a rare level of polish.
Planned Chaos

The album’s eight tracks build on one another, easing listeners into the skilful interweaving of multiple elements not typically strung together on Kenyan projects. The opening track Running starts with a crescendo of horns that indicates the big room atmosphere that permeates the project. It is loud but not in an annoying way. It invites the listener into a space where they are washed over by so many sonic shapes and grooves until it becomes an undeniably worthwhile experience. The horns then cut off into a sequence of drums that immediately reminds you that this is a Blinky Bill project at heart. While every individual part of Running is compelling, the opener lacks some of the creative cohesion that defines the rest of the album. From there, however, that concern quickly falls away as the record’s creativity gathers into an ever-strengthening current.

“Niko Hype"", the second track, is sparse and spacey, and the synths give the track an industrial, almost metal feel. Blinky Bill’s raps are rapid fire on here, simple but captivating: His unique flow, doled out in a much quicker tempo, meshes well with the staccato of MDQ’s voice shouting Niko Hype in the background, something that is both recognizable and unique.

On “Bazu,” MDQ steps in to remind listeners that her pen game is still as sharp as ever, landing memorable lines like,
<blockquote>
“Hii ni pombe gani
Hii pombe wasotaji hawapatangi”
To me, this is the album’s clearest standout, and the point where the collaboration fully locks into place.

Manchild, the producer known for his work with Chris Kaiga builds up a throbbing wall of keys atop a snappy drum loop, and like elsewhere, horn stabs punctuates the production, proof that anything Blinky Bill and MDQ touch is bound to carry a little bounce.

The project mostly settles into a moderate tempo, giving room for both rapid-fire rapping and slower, more melodic vocals, as best heard on “Sina Makosa.” The track stands out for its resistance to easy classification by genre or era: the drums, the immaculate Boutross feature, MDQ and Blinky Bill sing-rapping are all blended together with an electronic, funkified beat. This song perfectly encapsulates the promise of the project. Here are two of the most experienced artists in Kenya and they’re still pushing the envelope on what the music can become.

Dillie, the veteran producer, leaves his fingerprints all over the project, contributing to the majority of its production. His touch is best felt on “Keru” an introspective track that opens with guitar strings that can misdirect some before launching into a beat that is built on an anthemic tribal chant that fits the vibe of the track. The unstated Lisa Oduor- Noah feature on ""Aina Moja"" highlights the final act of the album, and not just because of Lisa’s ever present role in Blinky Bill’s and MDQ’s careers. MDQ’s verse steals the show here while Blinky Bill happily takes a backseat.
""Kila kitu nafanya inanichanganya
Ile kitu nikama nimepatikana""

This may be the album’s defining quality: even as two veterans of the scene, both artists effortlessly allow each other to take the lead throughout the project. Across the record, they keep building the case that neither is especially concerned with being the centre of attention, so long as they are in the middle of something new and different.
Verdict

This project feels both anticipated and unexpected. Its promise was always clear, given the duo’s long history of collaboration, but its sonic direction remained an open question until now. While this project is only a 28-minute platter of creativity, its many moving parts come together as a concise, unified whole: one that is almost always distinctive, and succeeds on far more levels than it falters. 628c75c5-d214-475f-abcf-913d16319e91,205955,how-afrohouse-found-a-second-home-in-nairobi,How Afrohouse Found a Second Home in Nairobi,null,"It is a Thursday night, the last day of April. I get to the club at 10.30 PM, which in the regular Nairobi logic means I am showing up embarrassingly early. The act I want to see will not touch the decks until well past midnight. That gives me time to nurse a drink, find a good spot near the speakers and ease into the night. That was the plan. I managed to slip inside just before the rain became unbearable, speaking with the familiar bouncers about the atrocious Nairobi weather. Once inside I am standing near the bar, drink in hand, and the dance floor is a heaving mass of bodies moving to the same deep pulse. A familiar bassline wraps around the room. Around me, I hear whispers. We might be at capacity. Someone says Rituals, the event I am at, filled up by ten. This is the new normal in Nairobi. Over the past few years, Afrohouse has stopped being a niche sound for Sunday afternoon lounges. It has become a permanent fixture of the city's nightlife. And on nights like this, when Rituals celebrates the Kenyan holders of the genre’s torch, you learn quickly that showing up early no longer means what it used to.
The Roots Of The Genre

But the music that fills this room did not start here. It started more than four thousand kilometres south of Nairobi, in the townships of Johannesburg and Pretoria, where a different kind of house music was taking shape. Afrohouse emerged in South Africa in the 1990s, layering traditional percussion and chants over the steady four on the floor beat of house music. It drew from kwaito, the post apartheid hybrid, and from deep house rhythms that had found their way to shanty towns like Soweto.

For years, this sound stayed home, slowly evolving as it interacted with different identities. Then came 2008. That year, a producer named DJ Mujava dropped ""Township Funk"", a giddy, two-note riff that zig zagged across the spectrum. A video surfaced on YouTube, featuring the song and quickly it was something to talk about on the music side of the internet. The label, This Is Music, stumbled upon the track on a music forum in a thread called ""African YouTube."" Warp Records picked it up for global release. The New York Times called it one of the biggest global dance hits of the year. As noted by Pitchfork, ""Township Funk"" paved an international path for a range of African and African diasporic music that followed in its wake.
It was the sound of the return to the dancefloor.

The figure who truly walked through that door and built the foundation of what the genre would later become was Black Coffee. Born in Mthatha, his one arm mixing technique, a consequence of a car accident at age 21, set him apart. He debuted his label Soulistic Music, collaborated with vocalists like Bucie and Zakes Bantwini, and by the time he played Coachella in 2019, the world was paying attention. He was not alone. Building on this solid foundation the sound began to travel outside South Africa, crossing borders until it eventually landed in Kenya.
The Bridge To Nairobi

It took some time for those Joburg sounds to travel north. But the first true explosion of South African dance music in Kenya did not come from Afrohouse at all. It came from Amapiano. When the pandemic hit in 2019 and clubs went dark, Amapiano spread like wildfire through streaming playlists, TikTok challenges and the occasional day parties that everyone wanted to be at (Remember Spasso Saturdays?). That log drum bassline, the jazzy piano stabs, the mid tempo swing that felt good whether you were in a crowd or by yourself. By the time clubs reopened, ‘piano was everywhere. Nairobi could not get enough. Every DJ had a playlist. Every party had at least one Amapiano set. It was the sound of the return to the dancefloor.

Amapiano being the flashier genre compared to the restraint of Afrohouse. DJs who had built their sets around Amapiano began digging backwards, finding the Black Coffee tracks, the Culoe De Song records, the early Black Motion cuts that had paved the way, and the likes. Afrohouse came even closer home with the release of “Umenitosha”, a smash hit by Kenyan singer Polaris and South African DJ Prince Kaybee. Crowds that had learned to love the log drum soon found themselves losing their minds to a rolling Afrohouse bassline at two in the morning. The pandemic was the start of a small wave that grew into a tsunami in the years that followed.

The underground collectives did the real work of bringing the soil to life. Kunye Records, founded by South African DJ Shimza during the global lockdowns of 2020, began as a series of streamed sets. It quickly grew into one of the most celebrated Afrohouse event series on the continent, with shows across Johannesburg, Cape Town and Nairobi. When Kunye touches down in Kenya, it transforms outdoor spaces into a cathedral of sound packed with fans, and somehow it always rains during Kunye. Kunye isn’t the only international brand with eyes on Nairobi. Descendants and Sound International touched down in the city in 2025, with support from local acts. Gondwana, founded by Nairobi DJs Suraj and Euggy, has spent nearly a decade establishing itself as the pillar of Kenya's Afrohouse movement. From small parties to a global label, Gondwana has already put Kenya on the electronic music map. Alongside them, Aduma has carved out a niche by creating spaces for emerging DJs to showcase their craft while making the genre accessible to as many people as possible while reshaping the city's electronic and Afrohouse scenes.

The venues that host these nights have become destinations in their own right. MUZE Club, started as the first venue in Nairobi dedicated to electronic music. It began with a 400 person capacity and a dream. Today, they have upgraded to a 1,500 capacity venue with three rooms, home to a crisp sound system that some say is one of the best in Africa. MUZE has broken into DJ Mag's Top 100 Clubs list and held its spot for years. Alongside them is KODA, on the same floor of the same building as MUZE. The two venues are like holy sites for fans of Afrohouse and a regular pilgrimage is demanded.

The artists at the heart of this ecosystem are the ones who turned a borrowed sound into something distinctly Kenyan. Producers like Suraj, Jack Rooster, Saint Evo and Euggy have been shaping the local scene from the ground up.. Euggy has built a reputation that takes him from Nairobi to Johannesburg, Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Jack Rooster, who helmed the Deeper Sounds Of Nairobi show was one of the pioneers who popularized African dance music to the greater Nairobi audience. On the global stage, Sofiya Nzau, one of the most recognizable vocalists in house music, made history in July 2024 as the first East African artist to perform at Tomorrowland in Belgium. Just months later, Idd Aziz became the first Kenyan to perform at Burning Man in Nevada.

What has made this explosion possible? I put the question to two DJs who have been very active in the scene. Onedown, a staple of the Nairobi electronic scene, credits the hardworking DJs who fought to be heard before the music was considered cool and trendy, the small communities that walked with them, and social media. Kamushez, another key figure, offered a longer reflection. ""The growth of the scene has also been based on various consistent factors,"" he told me. ""From my experience, when I started DJing I was fortunate enough to find existing structures that actively pushed for electronic music like Dawa Sesh, Santuri East Africa, venues like Captain Terrace on Sundays, Gondwana and Aduma. These spaces gave me the confidence to pursue a career in music. Also in the same breath, the growth of Amapiano really helped audiences and venues accept Afrohouse much faster. I really appreciate the space where the Kenyan electronic music scene is at right now. I feel it has been easier now more than ever to actualize ideas and experiences from just how receptive the audience has been to Afrohouse lately.""

The word that keeps coming up is export. Kenyan Afrohouse has developed its own flavour, a bright percussive sound that sits somewhere between the deep grooves of Johannesburg and the melodic sensibilities of East Africa. It is no longer just music that Kenyans dance to. It is music that the world is starting to discover. What started as a trickle of South African tracks on Nairobi dancefloors has become a flood. And the city is finally getting the recognition it deserves. As more than one person has said, Nairobi is the second home of Afrohouse in Africa.
Why Nairobi Embraced Afrohouse

So why Nairobi? Why not Dar es Salaam, Kampala or Lagos? The answer is partly about infrastructure, the clubs that took risks, the collectives that built communities, the DJs who refused to give up. But the deeper answer is about sound itself. There is something about

Afrohouse that fits the Kenyan ear. The genre is built on rolling percussion, deep basslines and melodic phrasing that does not demand you understand the language to feel the emotion. That percussive backbone, those layered drums that lock into a groove and refuse to let go, feels familiar to anyone who grew up listening to Benga, Rhumba or the rhythms of coastal taarab. It is not that Afrohouse sounds like those older genres. It is that the listening body already knows how to move to this kind of pattern.

This familiarity is also futuristic. Afrohouse is not nostalgia music. It is electronic, club ready, international in its references and collaborations. When a Kenyan DJ drops a track that samples a Luo chant or a Kikuyu proverb over a Johannesburg bassline, the crowd feels two things at once. A connection to home and a portal to the rest of the world. That duality is exactly what young urban Kenyans are living every day. We are here, but we are also online. We speak Sheng, English and whatever else gets the point across. We want music that reflects that complexity. Afrohouse embodies this state of mind perfectly.

There is also something about what the genre represents. For a generation coming of age in a country where the cost of living keeps climbing and the political news keeps getting heavier, Afrohouse offers a particular kind of escape. It is not the reckless escape of chemical excess or the numbing escape of scrolling through bad news. It is the escape of the body moving in sync with strangers, of sweat and bass and a room full of people who came for the same reason. To feel good. To forget for a few hours. To remember that joy is still possible. As Kamushez said, the audience has become receptive. People are hungry for this feeling.

The pandemic aftershock cannot be overstated. After months of lockdown, of Zoom parties and solo listening, the return to the dancefloor was a kind of rebirth. Amapiano gave people something familiar and new at the same time. Afrohouse gave them a deeper, longer, more textured journey. The clubs that survived, places like MUZE and The Alchemist, became something like cathedrals of sound. The DJs became prophets. And the congregation kept growing. Thursday nights started looking like Saturday nights. Capacity became a regular problem and that is a good problem to have.

What makes Nairobi the second home rather than just another city with a decent scene is the sense of ownership. South Africa birthed Afrohouse. But Kenya has raised a distinct branch of the family tree. The sound here is brighter, more melodic, touched by the same East African air that gave us Benga and Rhumba. Listen to a track by DJ Mura or Ally Fresh and you will hear it. The drums hit a little differently. The vocals, often in Kiswahili or Sheng, carry a different cadence. It is still Afrohouse but it is Kenyan Afrohouse. That distinction matters.

And the world is noticing. When Sofiya Nzau stepped onto the Tomorrowland stage, she was not just representing herself. She was representing a whole ecosystem of producers, DJs, promoters and dancers who had spent years building something from nothing. When Idd Aziz played at Burning Man, he carried the flag for every Kenyan who ever dreamed that their music could travel that far. The road from the shanty towns of South Africa to the halls of Nairobi nightclubs is long. But the road from Nairobi to the rest of the world is getting shorter by the day.

It started in the townships of Johannesburg, in taxicabs and the restless minds of producers who wanted to make something that felt ancestral and futuristic at once. It was carried north by hard drives and chance encounters, by DJs who refused to stop playing tracks that confused the crowds at first. It found a foothold during a pandemic when amapiano opened Kenyan ears to the deeper grooves of South African dance music. And then it exploded.
